items.title: From training clips to thirst traps: why athletes are turning to OnlyFans
items.summary:
A professional sports career does not guarantee wealth. And a growing number of athletes are turning to alternative streams of income

“I’m sick and tired of it.” Bart Swings tossed his jacket behind him. It was August 2025, the Winter Olympics were less than six months away, and the Belgian Olympic champion’s injured knee was not getting better. The clip, profanity and all, later ran on the Belgian evening news along with the weather and the football. But the injury update didn’t come from an interview – it was broadcast on the speed skater’s OnlyFans channel.

The subscription site, best known for porn dudes, cam girls and dubiously horny couples, has quietly assembled one of the stranger rosters in professional sport. The list, about 285 athletes deep, includes Olympic speed skaters and rowers, tennis players, surfers and golfers. And, despite its racy reputation, many of the athletes on OnlyFans are not putting out adult content.

Continue reading...

items.title: The unthinkable has come to pass: Tom Brady is a pretty good broadcaster
items.summary:
The former NFL quarterback was widely derided when he starter his job in the Fox booth. But he has shown a human side and explains the game beautifully

I have accidentally force-fed myself Tom Brady’s commentary as my primary means of watching the NFL this season. When my favorite team, the Steelers, hired Mike McCarthy as head coach, I lodged a silent protest by declining to spend the several hundred dollars needed to get NFL Sunday Ticket. I didn’t even splurge for RedZone. That means I’ve found myself watching Fox’s NFL broadcasts on a Sunday – often an underwhelming Cowboys game – where Brady is the color commentator in the network’s No 1 booth, alongside play-by-play man Kevin Burkhardt.

This two-and-a-half-month experiment has led me to an alarming conclusion, one I’d seen others reaching gradually over the last year but never taken too seriously myself. Recently, though, the truth has become unavoidable: Tom Brady is pretty good at his job. Gone are the days of the best quarterback of all time being hopelessly outmatched on TV. What has changed is that Brady now sounds like an actual human being.

Continue reading...
items.t: The unthinkable has come to pass: Tom Brady is a pretty good broadcaster

items.title: You have to laugh at LIV’s collapse but the saga reveals money is golf’s core value | Jonathan Liew
items.summary:
Why do rich powerful men love golf? Ultimately the sport exists in a world where the politics is assumed to be settled

Farewell, then, LIV Golf. As its original figurehead Greg Norman once so delicately put it, albeit in a slightly different context: we’ve all made mistakes, you learn from those mistakes, and you move forward. Forward – in LIV’s case – to bankruptcy court and the start of liquidation proceedings some time in January 2027. And not without a certain irony, in the sense that Norman’s cherished project, established over a cacophony of human rights concerns, ended up getting dismembered and terminated on the orders of the Saudi government. Life moves on you pretty fast.

Perhaps the funniest part of LIV’s protracted demise – unless you count the television viewing figures – has been the last seven months, after Saudi Arabia abruptly pulled the plug on the seemingly abundant flow of money that had fuelled its astonishing rise. Suddenly LIV’s chief executive, Scott O’Neil, was forced to take his begging bowl up and down midtown Manhattan, panhandling for change, drawing up entirely conceptual revenue forecasts, pretending for all the world that this was an actual, real-life business proposition; a legitimate going concern with profits and a bottom line and a plan for the future.

Continue reading...
items.t: You have to laugh at LIV’s collapse but the saga reveals money is golf’s core value | Jonathan Liew

In many ways, there are striking parallels between the Manchester United relegated in 1974 and the Manchester United sitting in the relegation zone at this stage of the season for the first time in 40 years. A legendary manager leaves, his shadow remains; with boardroom dithering and uncertainty, his replacements churn and burn as the club slide over several years.

Sir Matt Busby stepped aside as manager of the 1968 European Cup-winning side, but stayed on as a director, just as Sir Alex Ferguson did, watching from the Old Trafford directors’ box as successors tried and failed.

items.title: Shame is the only punishment in Australian cricket’s sandpaper scandal | Geoff Lemon
items.summary:
The time for formal measures has passed but all involved have betrayed the trust of a country whose Test team is sacred

Cry havoc. But Cameron Bancroft did not let anything slip, not after close to a decade of keeping his mouth firmly shut. It was a deliberate, considered and lengthy deed of revelation that the former Test opening bat chose to publish in the West Australian newspaper on Wednesday, claiming to finally fill in a wealth of detail around Australian cricket’s 2018 cheating scandal that so many others seem to have gone to such lengths to keep concealed.

It was also a devastating repudiation of Pat Cummins, a teammate of equivalent juniority to Bancroft during their few months playing together, but now the Test captain, who had delivered his own manifesto in spoken form at a press conference last week. That version of events, in which Cummins was adamant that he had never been aware of any kind of ball-tampering in Australian colours, was what pushed Bancroft from silence to speech. “It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone,” Bancroft wrote. “What I saw, experienced and lived with not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously.”
items.t: Shame is the only punishment in Australian cricket’s sandpaper scandal | Geoff Lemon

items.title: Rugby brain injury lawsuits again on brink of collapse over medical documents delay
items.summary:
• Claimants’ legal team argues for extension until January

  • Future of case rests on decisions of the two judges

After six years of interminable and expensive legal argument, the two lawsuits involving hundreds of brain-damaged rugby players appear to be on the brink of collapsing.

The lead counsel representing the players, Paul Downes KC, had conceded in June that the claimants were in the “last-chance saloon” after repeatedly missing court-mandated deadlines for the disclosure of documents to the defendants. Having done so again this October, they now appear to be somewhere out beyond it.

items.title: Alexander Zverev notified of abuse lawsuit by ex-partner during ATP Finals
items.summary:
• Men’s world No 1 allegedly violated terms of settlement

  • Lawyers say Zverev will ‘defend himself against lawsuit’

Alexander Zverev was officially notified of a lawsuit filed by his former partner during the middle of the season-ending ATP Finals on Wednesday. The latest legal case against the men’s world No 1 brought by the mother of the former couple’s daughter alleges that Zverev violated the terms of an out-of-court settlement between the pair after the woman accused him of assaulting her.

The lawsuit brought by Brenda Patea in Germany takes issue with Zverev reportedly saying in an interview with the French sports daily L’Equipe earlier this year that “it has been proven that the accusations were false” and “my innocence has been proven”.

Continue reading...
items.t: Alexander Zverev notified of abuse lawsuit by ex-partner during ATP Finals

items.title: Prem Rugby fires starting gun on 12-team expansion plan with £20m entry fee
items.summary:
• Interested clubs have until 1 February to come forward

  • Prem chief is in US attempting to find potential investors

Prem Rugby has fired the starting gun on expanding to 12 teams by formally asking interested clubs to come forward by February. The chief executive, Simon Massie-Taylor, is in the United States attempting to woo investors, with the Prem determined to add two more teams to its ranks for the 2029-30 competition.

The previous top-flight sides Worcester Warriors, who won last season’s rebranded Champ, and London Irish – who have signalled their intention to return to the second tier as soon as next season – are among those expected to throw their hats into the ring, while the Welsh Rugby Union has sent a letter outlining a desire for clubs to join the Prem and create an Anglo-Welsh league.

Continue reading...
items.t: Prem Rugby fires starting gun on 12-team expansion plan with £20m entry fee

items.title: Reid Wiseman, the astronaut shooting for the moon in F1 with Mercedes
items.summary:
Nasa crew member is fast seeing the similarities between flying Artemis II into lunar orbit and the F1 team’s drive for sporting brilliance

There are characters aplenty within Formula One, a sport that attracts the larger‑than-life, and at the sharp end it can be a parade ground for swaggering egos. Yet the newest addition to the paddock is a man whose quietly spoken, understated thoughtfulness and insight are compelling. Now part of the Mercedes team, Reid Wiseman has been to the moon and with it brings a perspective like no other.

Wiseman was one of four astronauts, alongside Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen, who completed the Artemis II lunar flyby in April. Last month Wiseman, the mission’s commander, became an ambassador for Mercedes’ F1 team, formalising a relationship that had been growing over several years, to the delight of his daughter, Katey, a fan of the newly crowned world champion, Kimi Antonelli.

Continue reading...
items.t: Reid Wiseman, the astronaut shooting for the moon in F1 with Mercedes

items.title: Netflix, Fox and the $2bn bid for the 2030 World Cup that could reshape live sports
items.summary:
The battle for the US TV rights to the tournament will pit the traditional broadcaster against the ‘whatever-it-takes’ streamer. It could be a tipping point in the industry

The awarding of broadcast rights in the United States for this year’s World Cup was a cut-price deal to avoid legal action from the existing rights holders, Fox Sports. This week’s tender process for the 2030 tournament will be anything but.

Media rights and broadcast experts canvassed by the Guardian in the US and Europe are united in agreement that Fifa will benefit from the most competitive and expensive auction in the competition’s history. It is expected to fetch between $1.5bn (£1.13bn) and $2bn, with some predicting the outcome could be a landmark moment for the sports and entertainment industry.

Continue reading...
items.t: Netflix, Fox and the $2bn bid for the 2030 World Cup that could reshape live sports

items.title: Child doping isn’t just cheating – it’s a global epidemic of abuse and exploitation | Sean Ingle
items.summary:
Surveys estimate 10 million minors globally use banned performance-enhancing drugs but suppliers are rarely brought to justice

Of all the many stories in Doping Top Secret: Children, a powerful new documentary from the German investigative team that helped expose massive Russian cheating in sport over a decade ago, one keeps replaying in my mind.

It involves an East German champion, who breaks his silence half a century on from his Olympic triumph to reveal how being pumped full of anabolic steroids at a young age accelerated his sexual development and, he believes, dramatically altered his behaviour and those of his teammates. “The system abused me as a young person for the good of the state,” says Hans-Georg Aschenbach, who won ski-jump gold in Innsbruck in 1976. Although nothing can prepare you for what he says about how the drugs affected his libido, and particularly what he would sometimes do before he jumped off a large ramp.

Continue reading...
items.t: Child doping isn’t just cheating – it’s a global epidemic of abuse and exploitation | Sean Ingle

items.title: Jack Grealish recalls a golden age of mavericks – but football has moved on
items.summary:
Everton forward has magical talent and popularity to burn, but has come up against hard reality of the modern game

Thomas Tuchel has never called up the player he once claimed to love “everything about”. The reason for Jack Grealish’s omission from Tuchel’s first England squad in March 2025 was given as “he simply has no rhythm”.

Catch a falling star? Last month Grealish was suspended by Everton for three matches after “a breach of club discipline”. Suggestions his loan from Manchester City might be cancelled were calmed by David Moyes. Last week, Grealish played in a behind-closed-doors friendly against Derby before issuing an Instagram statement: “I want to apologise to the fans and everyone at the club for not being able to help the team the last few weeks.” Amid tabloid tales of karaoke nights and extended socialising, how close is the former boy wonder, now 31, to blowing it?

Continue reading...
items.t: Jack Grealish recalls a golden age of mavericks – but football has moved on
